source.title: Deforming the Loss Surface
source.authors: Liang-Ming Chen; Long Jin; Xiujuan Du; Shuai Li; Mei Liu

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplementary material are present; the final figure pages are flattened, but the relevant experiment tables and text are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether loss-surface deformation changes measured flatness and held-out image-classification accuracy, using its own training intervention and loss-curve visualizations rather than the original claim versions' measurements.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the deformation intervention's reported loss-curve findings and test-accuracy comparisons. The simulated loss-surface figures are described in text but are not natural-data model results; cited prior studies' findings are not rows. Table 1 and Table 6 compare deformation functions with scheduler settings, but are omitted because these are method comparisons rather than outcomes of the claim's object.
record.test_reason: The study uses the flat-minima/generalization premise to design a training method and evaluates its loss-curve flatness and classification accuracy. It does not test V7's magnitude-aware perturbation measure against training–test gaps or competing measures, and it tests none of V1–V6 or V8.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase broadly matches the conclusion: the authors argue that deformation helps filter sharp minima and improves generalization, with reported gains up to 1.46 percentage points. Table 2 assigns that largest gain to PreResNet-20 on CIFAR-100, although the abstract and introduction incorrectly name ResNet-20. All Table 2–3 comparisons improve numerically, but Table 6 includes deformation settings that worsen accuracy; no repeated-run uncertainty establishes statistical significance.
record.recipe_differences: Introduces a loss deformation function into SGDM training and reports loss-curve visualizations and natural-image test accuracy; it does not test the claim versions' interventions or measures.
record.method_sensitivity: The loss-curve flatness changes with deformation function and its coefficients; text says larger AP a1 yields flatter minima. Test accuracy results use different deformation functions across models.

fits_no_version.finding: The deformation settings reported in Tables 2 and 3 improve classification accuracy over their corresponding original models; the gains range from 0.02 to 1.46 percentage points.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Selected loss-deformation settings can improve SGDM classification performance on the tested CNNs and image datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 3 describes increasingly flat filter-normalized loss curves as AP a1 increases, but Table 6 reports corresponding accuracies of 69.53%, 69.60%, 70.67%, and 69.19%, against 69.76% originally. Visual flatness and accuracy therefore do not improve monotonically together.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For ResNet-20 on CIFAR-100, deformation changes visual loss-curve flatness, while accuracy depends on the deformation coefficients.

fits_no_version.finding: Quadratic deformation produces a visually sharp minimum and accuracy of 69.60%, versus 69.76% for the original model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some loss-deformation settings yield sharper minima and lower classification accuracy than original SGDM.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates or repeated-run variability are reported in the supplied text. Flatness is illustrated with loss curves rather than a magnitude-aware perturbation metric, and the reported test accuracies have no paired training accuracies, so they do not measure training-test gaps.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 scheduler comparisons and Table 6 learning-rate-scheduler comparisons are omitted as comparisons among training methods, not results directly measuring the claim versions' named behaviors. Simulated two-parameter loss-surface visualizations are not natural-data model outcomes.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label versus random-label held-out performance.
Width sweeps beyond the width required for interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizers under specified tuning budgets.
Batch-size effects under matched epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout interventions and their dependence on data size or augmentation.

Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance versus training–test error gaps among similarly fitted networks, including ranking against norm and margin measures. Filter-normalized loss curves provide related visual evidence, but no such measurement or ranking is reported.
Removal of memorized examples versus matched random removals followed by retraining.

record.verdict_notes: R6–R25 are correctly transcribed method-performance comparisons, rather than evidence for the listed versions. All rows remain unlinked. Table 6 is explicitly declared in rows_left_out, so its additional results do not require missing entries. The theoretical discussion of pacGen and sharpness does not establish or refute V7's specified empirical relationship.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or comparison of natural-label and random-label generalization.
No network-width sweep or test of widening beyond interpolation.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison or test of local connectivity.
Only SGDM is used; adaptive optimizers are not compared.
No batch-size comparison; batch sizes are experimental settings only.

Tests loss-curve flatness under deformation and held-out classification accuracy, but does not compute magnitude-aware sharpness or compare it with norm- and margin-based measures; no CIFAR-10 or SVHN results without augmentation.
No removal of memorized examples or retraining comparison.

rows.subject: ResNet-20
rows.operation_detail: Trained with δ(ℓ) = 0.5ℓ² and SGDM; loss curves near the resulting minimum are visualized.

conditions.value: random crop and random horizontal flip

rows.measure: Loss-curve flatness near the minimum; text says this setting falls into a sharp minimum and performs worse than the original model.
rows.baseline: Original model loss curve; quantitative baseline not stated.
rows.value: Sharp minimum; performs worse than the original model.
rows.note: The result is about ordinary loss-curve flatness, not magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness or a measured training-test gap.
rows.check: Filter-normalized loss-curve visualization does not measure V7's sharpness–gap relationship. Table 6 supplies the omitted accuracy comparison: 69.60% versus 69.76%.
